question: Schematic gas-volume diagram; vessel sizes are not drawn to scale. The balanced equation is: H₂+Cl₂→ 2HCl
diagramSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 340 110" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <rect x="8" y="18" width="86" height="60" rx="5" fill="#DCEBFF" stroke="#3569A8" strokeWidth="1.5"/>
    <rect x="108" y="18" width="86" height="60" rx="5" fill="#FCE5CE" stroke="#C66A24" strokeWidth="1.5"/>

    <text x="51" y="39" fontSize="13" textAnchor="middle" fill="#204E85">H₂</text>

    <text x="51" y="96" fontSize="10.5" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Reactant 1</text>
    <text x="151" y="96" fontSize="10.5" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Reactant 2</text>
    <text x="281" y="96" fontSize="10.5" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Same T and P</text>
  </svg>
explanation:
The volume ratio is 1:1:2.

- 20 cm³ of chlorine consumes 20 cm³ of hydrogen.
- Hydrogen remaining =30-20=10 cm³.
- HCl formed =2×20=40 cm³.

Therefore,


V_{final}=40+10=50 cm³


The tempting answer, 40 cm³, counts only the HCl produced and ignores the unreacted hydrogen.

title: Avogadro’s law and the number of atoms
question: All three jars are at identical temperature and pressure. What is the ratio of the total number of atoms in the CO₂ jar to that in the H₂ jar?

<svg viewBox="0 0 460 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">
    <text x="230" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">Avogadro's Law: Equal Volumes at Identical T & P</text>
    <!-- Jar 1: O2 -->
    <g transform="translate(60, 45)">
      <rect x="0" y="0" width="55" height="85" rx="4" fill="#eff6ff" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>

    </g>

    <g transform="translate(280, 45)">
      <rect x="0" y="0" width="55" height="85" rx="4" fill="#fef2f2" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="1.8"/>
      <text x="27" y="45" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="800" fill="#991b1b">CO₂</text>
      <text x="27" y="65" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="#dc2626">N molecules</text>
      <text x="27" y="105" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" font-weight="800" fill="#dc2626">3N atoms</text>
    </g>
    <text x="230" y="170" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#334155">Equal volumes contain equal numbers of MOLECULES, but atom ratio depends on atomicity</text>
  </svg>
explanation:
By Avogadro’s law, equal gas volumes at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

Let each jar contain N molecules.

- H₂ contains 2N atoms.
- CO₂ contains 3N atoms.

Therefore,


(Atoms in CO₂ / Atoms in H₂)
=(3N / 2N)=frac32


The tempting answer 1:1 confuses equal numbers of molecules with equal numbers of atoms.

title: A complete mole-conversion pathway
question: Given: C = 12, O = 16; Avogadro’s number =6.022×10^ mol^; molar volume at STP =22.4 L mol^. Which sequence correctly gives the moles, number of molecules and volume at STP, respectively?

    <rect x="91" y="20" width="70" height="56" rx="6" fill="#E4F5EA" stroke="#43845A"/>

    <g fontSize="10.5" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">
      <text x="39" y="39">Mass</text><text x="39" y="56" fontWeight="bold">11 g</text>
      <text x="126" y="39">Moles</text><text x="126" y="56">?</text>
      <text x="214" y="38">Molecules</text><text x="214" y="56">?</text>
      <text x="301" y="38">Volume</text><text x="301" y="56">? L</text>

    <text x="214" y="89" fontSize="9.5" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Avogadro's number</text>

explanation:
Molar mass of CO₂:


M_r=12+2(16)=44


Moles:


n=(11 / 44)=0.25 mol


Molecules:


N=0.25(6.022×10^{23})
=1.5055×10^{23}


Volume at STP:


V=0.25(22.4)=5.6 L


The tempting option C doubles both the mole and volume values. The correct starting mass is only one-quarter of the molar mass.

title: Interpreting a mass-versus-moles graph
question: Given: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, N = 14. Which gas could be represented by line R?
diagramSvg:

    <line x1="42" y1="120" x2="178" y2="120" stroke="#8AA9CC" strokeDasharray="3 3"/>

    <path d="M42 145 L178 66" stroke="#D17736" strokeWidth="2.5" fill="none"/>
    <text x="184" y="123" fontSize="11" fill="#4676B9">P: 8 g</text>
    <text x="184" y="97" fontSize="11" fill="#298A54">Q: 16 g</text>
    <text x="184" y="69" fontSize="11" fill="#D17736">R: 22 g</text>
    <text x="35" y="158" fontSize="10" textAnchor="end" fill="currentColor">0</text>
    <text x="178" y="158" fontSize="10" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">0.5</text>

    <text x="15" y="82" fontSize="10" transform="rotate(-90 15 82)" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Mass (g)</text>
  </svg>
explanation:
The slope of a mass-versus-moles line is the molar mass:


M=(Mass / Moles)
=(22 / 0.5)=44 g mol^{-1}


For CO₂,


M=12+2(16)=44 g mol^{-1}


Therefore, line R represents CO₂. The tempting option O₂ has a molar mass of 32 g mol⁻¹, not 44 g mol⁻¹.

title: Identifying the unreacted gas from a volume table
question: The balanced equation is CH₄+2O₂→ CO₂+2H_2O(g) Given: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16. What volume of methane remains unreacted?
diagramSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 340 118" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <rect x="3" y="7" width="334" height="105" rx="5" fill="none" stroke="#9CA3AF"/>
    <line x1="3" y1="36" x2="337" y2="36" stroke="#9CA3AF"/>
    <line x1="3" y1="74" x2="337" y2="74" stroke="#9CA3AF"/>
    <line x1="86" y1="7" x2="86" y2="112" stroke="#9CA3AF"/>
    <line x1="169" y1="7" x2="169" y2="112" stroke="#9CA3AF"/>
    <line x1="252" y1="7" x2="252" y2="112" stroke="#9CA3AF"/>
    <g fontSize="10.5" textAnchor="middle" fill="currentColor">
      <text x="44" y="26">CH₄</text><text x="128" y="26">O₂</text><text x="210" y="26">CO₂</text><text x="294" y="26">H₂O(g)</text>
      <text x="44" y="58">1 vol</text><text x="128" y="58">2 vol</text><text x="210" y="58">1 vol</text><text x="294" y="58">2 vol</text>
      <text x="44" y="96" fontWeight="bold">45 cm³</text><text x="128" y="96" fontWeight="bold">80 cm³</text><text x="210" y="96">?</text><text x="294" y="96">?</text>
    </g>
  </svg>
explanation:
The equation requires two volumes of O₂ per volume of CH₄.

The 80 cm³ of O₂ can consume:


V_{CH₄,reacted}=(80 / 2)=40 cm³


Therefore,


V_{CH₄,left}=45-40=5 cm³


**Correction check:** Option A is therefore the correct numerical result, not D. The correct answer for this question is **A**.

explanation:
The volume ratio is 1:3:2.

30 cm³ of H₂ reacts with:


(30 / 3)=10 cm³ of N₂


The corresponding ammonia volume is:


10×2=20 cm³

options.text: Equal masses of all gases react in equal volumes at the same temperature and pressure.
The volumes of reacting gases and gaseous products bear simple whole-number ratios when measured at the same temperature and pressure.
Equal volumes of different gases contain equal masses at the same temperature and pressure.
The volume of a gas is always proportional to its mass, irrespective of the gas involved.

explanation:
Gay-Lussac’s law states that gaseous reactants and gaseous products combine in simple whole-number volume ratios when measured under identical conditions of temperature and pressure. The law concerns volumes, not equal masses. Option C is tempting because equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules, but different gases have different molecular masses.
